title: What the homepage has to prove for an architecture studio
metaTitle: What an architecture studio homepage must prove
excerpt: An architecture studio homepage should show built work, name the constraint, and offer a way to start a project conversation. A fullscreen render with no words fails that client.
alt: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops, a working session for deciding which built project a client should see first.
caption: Sorting the first screen before anyone writes a slogan. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first screen show?
faqs.answer: A photograph of something the practice has built, the project name, and one sentence that names the constraint. A client who is judging taste before competence needs those three facts before a manifesto or a film. The way to start a project conversation should be visible on that same screen, including on a phone.

faqs.question: Can a young practice lead with a render?
faqs.answer: Lead with the best built work you have, even if it is a small alteration or a single room. If a current project is still on paper, show it later and label the drawing or the render as such. A first screen that is only a cinematic image, with no project name and no limit, gives a careful client nothing solid to judge.

faqs.question: How many projects belong on the homepage?
faqs.answer: Three is enough when each one names a different constraint and a decision. The longer story belongs on the project page. A homepage that tries to show the whole archive asks the client to curate the practice for you.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
An architecture studio homepage has one job for a client who is judging taste before competence: show built work, name the constraint, and offer a way to start a project conversation. A fullscreen render with no words fails that buyer. Taste without a decision is a mood, and a mood does not say whether you can take their site.

Write the page in that order. A picture of something you built. The limit that shaped it. A clear way to begin. The rest of the site can stay quiet once those three are obvious on the first screen.

## The first ten seconds

A client who hires an architect often decides with their eyes before they decide with a brief. They have seen a lot of dusk shots. They are asking a blunt question: have these people built something, and was it hard in a way that resembles my problem?

Nielsen Norman Group's research on [how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) found that visitors often leave within 10 to 20 seconds. A clear value proposition in the first 10 seconds is what earns a longer look. On this page the value proposition is not a slogan about timeless space. It is a building, a room, or a detail, with the constraint named beside it.

That constraint might be a steep site, a heritage overlay, a party wall, a flood level, or a budget that ruled out the first scheme. Name one. A client with a similar limit recognizes themselves. A client with a different limit still learns that the practice works from limits. That is what competence looks like before anyone has read a process diagram.

Put the project name where it can be read without a click. "House on a lane" is a start. "House on a lane, held to a single retaining wall the planner would allow" is the sentence that does the job. You do not need a paragraph in the hero. You need the fact that changes how the picture is read.

[Google's helpful content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a page has a primary purpose, and whether it was made for people who might come to you directly. The purpose here is to help a future client judge the work. A page built to impress other architects, or to collect awards in a ticker, misses that person.

## Built work, with the constraint named

Lead with work that exists in the world. A photograph of a finished room. A facade in ordinary daylight. A plan only when the plan is the decision you need them to see. Renders can sit later, labeled as renders, when the project is not built and the client needs to know that. The first image should not ask them to guess whether the building is real.

Sequence a few projects, not a reel. Three is enough on the homepage if each one names a different kind of limit. A new house, an alteration, an interior. Or three houses, if houses are the practice, each with a different rule. The point is a range of judgment. A range of styles, with no limits named, still looks like a mood board.

For each project, use the same small structure:

- A picture of the built thing.
- The project name and the place, as specific as you are willing to be.
- One sentence on the constraint.
- One sentence on the decision.

Stop there on the homepage. The long story belongs on the proof page. The homepage is the index of judgment. If a visitor wants the stair detail, the project page is one click away. If they only needed to know you can work on a tight urban plot, they already have it.

If a project cannot be named, say why in plain language, or leave it off the first screen. Anonymous hero images teach the visitor that the work is a texture. A client judging taste before competence will enjoy the texture and still not trust you with a site they have spent two years trying to buy.

A public reference for this kind of specificity is Thomas Bewick, an editorial heritage site where the craft is shown with its context. The architecture version is stricter, because the photograph is the thing the client is buying with their confidence. The words have to be precise enough that they could retell the project to their partner that evening.

## The words under the picture

Write the way you would explain the project in the first meeting. Short sentences. Materials, spans, and rules when they matter. "The stair sits in the only wall the planner would allow" is a decision. "A dialogue between light and stone" can be true and still tell them nothing they can use.

Keep one voice. If the homepage is quiet and specific, the captions should be quiet and specific. A sudden paragraph of manifesto under a careful photograph feels like a second practice has taken over the page.

The visible title of the page can be the practice name. The sentence beside the first project does the explaining. The title element in the browser can be plainer still, so someone who searched for residential work can tell the page is about built houses. One obvious heading is enough. Several slogans competing for the hero is how a page becomes a poster.

Leave awards out of that first sentence. An award can be a footnote on the project if it is true and if the client would care. It is not the constraint. The client still needs to know what was hard, and what you did about it.

Read the caption out loud. If you run out of breath, it is a paragraph doing a sentence's job. If a colleague who did not work on the job cannot repeat the constraint after one reading, the sentence is still about the practice, not about the building.

## A way to start a project conversation

The third part of the job is the path. Name it in the client's language. "Start a project" is clear. "Let's collaborate" is fog. The path can be a short note, a link to a contact page, or a time to talk. Say what the conversation is for: to hear the site, the rough use, and whether the practice is a fit.

Say what you want them to have ready, in one line. An address. Whether they own it. A rough sense of use. Whether a builder is already involved. You do not need the full brief on the homepage. You need them to know the conversation is about a real project.

Repeat that path once more after the work. A client who has scrolled the projects and is convinced should not have to hunt. A client who is not convinced should not be trapped in a modal, a newsletter gate, or a film they cannot skip.

On a Hanabi project, that order is the scope: first screen, a few projects with constraints, one conversation path. The studio designs and builds, so the page is not a folder of pictures waiting for someone else to interpret. [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) cover a marketing site of that kind, from the structure in Figma through a Next.js build the practice can keep. The page stays small on purpose. A small page that tells the truth is easier to look after than a long one that performs taste.

State the limit of this page. It cannot close a complex civic commission, and it should not pretend to. It can earn the first conversation with a private client or a developer who is still choosing who to call. That is the job. Treat anything more as a bonus.

## What a fullscreen render does

A fullscreen render with no words is the failure this buyer hits most often. It reassures the people inside the practice. It looks like the images on the studio wall. It also withholds the two facts the client came for: that the work was built, and that a constraint was handled.

The render may be beautiful. Beauty is not the missing piece. The missing piece is a decision a stranger can retell. Without a project name, a place, and a limit, the image could belong to any office with the same renderer and the same tree library. The client cannot tell you apart, so they cannot choose you.

If the practice is young and the built archive is thin, use the best built thing you have. A kitchen. A stair. A fit-out. Then show one in-progress project with the drawing and the constraint, labeled honestly. Thin and true beats a cinematic image that could be anyone's. A client commissioning a first house is often relieved to see a practice that will say what is standing and what is still on paper.

Move the film, if you have one, below the first project. Autoplay with no caption is the same problem in motion. Sound is worse. A person comparing three practices on a phone in a cafe will mute you by leaving.

## Order the page, then stop

A practical order:

1. One built project, large, with the constraint in the first sentence.
2. Two more projects, same structure, different limits.
3. A short line on who does the work, with a link onward, not a biography.
4. One path to start a project conversation.
5. A way to see the rest of the work.

Then stop. A journal, a press list, and a statement of values can exist on the site. They do not belong above the work. The helpful-content test is plain: would a client who came to you directly, with a site in mind, learn enough to take the next step? If they would leave to keep searching for what you actually build, the page is not finished.

Check it on a phone before you fall in love with the desktop crop. The first screen still has to hold the picture, the constraint, and the path. If the crop turns the building into an abstract band and the sentence falls below the fold, the desktop composition has decided the page for the wrong device.

Keep the type large enough to read at arm's length, and keep the button's words the same in the header and at the end of the page. "Start a project" in the corner and "Inquire" at the bottom are two doors. Pick one label and use it everywhere.

## After the homepage, the fee

The homepage is the proof in miniature. Once a careful client believes you have built something, the next private question is usually money. They are not ready to do arithmetic. They want to know whether the practice is even in range, and what a fee is supposed to include.

That is the job of [a pricing page for an architecture studio](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-an-architecture-studio). Read it when the first screen is starting to tell the truth and the fee is still a conversation you rebuild from scratch on every call.
